articles.body: Services Top Right Tropical Shipping adds St. Croix to Canada Express service November 13, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Tropical Shipping has expanded its Canada Express container service with the addition of St. Croix in the US Virgin Islands, extending the route’s coverage between Canada, Florida and the Caribbean. According to DynaLiners, the revised service is operated by two container vessels, each with a capacity of approximately 1,100 TEU, connecting Halifax with Palm Beach and several Caribbean destinations. The updated port rotation will be: Halifax – Palm Beach – San Juan – St. Thomas – St. Maarten – St. Croix – Halifax. The addition of St. Croix provides another port connection within the Canada Express network, alongside the existing calls in Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands and St. Maarten. Tropical Shipping already maintains operations in St. Croix through its wider Caribbean shipping network. The latest adjustment therefore extends the island’s coverage within the Canada Express service rather than establishing an entirely new destination for the carrier. The revised rotation retains Halifax as its Canadian gateway and Palm Beach as its Florida call, while expanding the service’s Caribbean port coverage to four destinations. articles.title: Nikkiso Delivers Dry Dock Overhaul for LNG Tanker
articles.summary: Nikkiso Clean Energy & Industrial Gases Group (Nikkiso CE&IG) has successfully completed a dry-dock maintenance project for the LNG tanker Ekaputra 1, carrying out the overhaul of seven cryogenic pumps in only 10 days. The work was performed…
articles.body: Nikkiso Delivers Dry Dock Overhaul for LNG Tanker Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 © Nikkiso CE&IG Nikkiso Clean Energy & Industrial Gases Group (Nikkiso CE&IG) has successfully completed a dry-dock maintenance project for the LNG tanker Ekaputra 1, carrying out the overhaul of seven cryogenic pumps in only 10 days. The work was performed for vessel owner Humolco by Nikkiso CE&IG’s Cryogenic Services Business Unit during the tanker’s scheduled dry dock window at PaxOcean shipyard in Batam, Indonesia. The scope included the overhaul of five large cargo pumps and two spray pumps, which all form part of the vessel’s LNG cargo handling operations. Completing seven pump overhauls within a 10-day dry-dock window required careful planning and coordination among Nikkiso CE&IG’s Cryogenic Services team, specialized subcontractors and the shipyard. Nikkiso coordinated personnel, parts and other resources in advance to keep the project on schedule, with all seven pumps overhauled, reinstalled, and recommissioned.

articles.title: Port of Hamburg records slight decline
articles.summary: The Port of Hamburg steadied its cargo handling in the third quarter of 2026, partially offsetting the declines of the first half. Total throughput at Germany’s largest seaport reached 84.5 million tonnes in the first nine months, 2.6% below the same period last year. The shortfall stems mainly from weather-related...
articles.body: The Port of Hamburg steadied its cargo handling in the third quarter of 2026, partially offsetting the declines of the first half. Total throughput at Germany’s largest seaport reached 84.5 million tonnes in the first nine months, 2.6% below the same period last year. The shortfall stems mainly from weather-related losses at the start of the year, disruption in the global oil market following the war in Iran and, most recently, strikes. Extensive modernisation work at the container terminals also weighed on results, but it is expected to strengthen the port’s performance and competitiveness and lay the foundations for future growth. Container throughput improved markedly in the third quarter compared with the end of the first half. Over the nine months the port handled 6.1 million TEU, down 2.8% in TEU and 2.6% in tonnes. TEU volumes rose with Singapore (+9.3%), India (+7.8%), Finland (+15.7%) and Sri Lanka (+3.7%). Persistent trade barriers continue to hamper trade with the USA (-9.8%), while volume with China, the port’s largest trading partner, is almost back at last year’s level (-0.6%). Many of the declines visible at the end of the second quarter were partly recovered during the third. Bulk cargo totalled 23.9 million tonnes, down 2.6%. Dry bulk continued to grow, up 1.7% on a significant recovery in grain exports and ore imports, partially offsetting a 13.3% fall in liquid bulk. In other general cargo and vehicles, a positive third quarter reversed the earlier downward trend, with the segment now up 2% at a total of 853 thousand tonnes.

articles.title: Neptune Pacific advances vessel deployments on MICROPAC and INTRAPAC services
articles.summary: Neptune Pacific has brought forward the deployment of ICS Silver Lining on its MICROPAC service and the redeployment of Southern Pearl to its INTRAPAC service, introducing additional cargo capacity across both Central Pacific trades ahead of the peak season. Under the revised arrangements, Southern Pearl will join...
articles.body: Neptune Pacific has brought forward the deployment of ICS Silver Lining on its MICROPAC service and the redeployment of Southern Pearl to its INTRAPAC service, introducing additional cargo capacity across both Central Pacific trades ahead of the peak season. Under the revised arrangements, Southern Pearl will join the INTRAPAC service as voyage 2611, calling at Funafuti, Apia and Wallis and Futuna. The vessel is scheduled to arrive in Funafuti on 19 November, Apia on 24 November, Wallis on 25 November and Futuna on 30 November. Cargo exported from Lautoka to Wallis and Futuna, currently carried aboard Capitaine Wallis voyage 2611, will be transferred to Southern Pearl in Apia. Meanwhile, ICS Silver Lining will enter the MICROPAC service as voyage 2609, loading cargo in Suva before proceeding to Tarawa, Majuro and Christmas Island (Kiritimati). The vessel is scheduled to call at Suva on 21 November, Tarawa on 27 November, Majuro on 3 December and Kiritimati on 12 December. Lautoka export cargo currently aboard Southern Pearl voyage 2609 will be transferred to ICS Silver Lining in Suva. Following the transitional voyages, Southern Pearl will resume the regular INTRAPAC rotation from voyage 2612, while ICS Silver Lining will return to the standard MICROPAC rotation from voyage 2610. The carrier said the accelerated deployments would provide additional cargo capacity to accommodate peak season demand across both services. Neptune Pacific also acknowledged that the revised arrangements would result in cargo disruptions and advised affected customers to contact its customer service team or local representatives for assistance.

Join the leading maritime news network FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Global oil markets are beginning to recover from the Iran war, but shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, with vessel traffic roughly 65% below pre-conflict levels and tanker attacks continuing across the region. Separate reports released Friday by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) highlight the uneven recovery in energy trade nearly nine months after the conflict began. The IEA said global oil supplies are on track to exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, reversing its previous forecast of a deficit as Persian Gulf producers restore disrupted exports. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, climbed to 18.4 million barrels per day in October, just 26% below pre-war levels. Crude shipments accounted for much of the recovery, reaching 15 million barrels per day, or about 82% of pre-war volumes. Yet the rebound in oil shipments has not translated into a broader recovery in vessel traffic. Hormuz Traffic Remains Deeply Disrupted In its latest weekly assessment, UKMTO reported 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits through the Strait of Hormuz, with overall traffic still approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. The figures combine AIS-tracked vessel movements with U.S.-reported facilitated transits, including ships operating without broadcasting AIS signals. UKMTO cautioned that it could not independently verify the U.S. figures. The security situation remains dangerous. UKMTO documented eight maritime security incidents during its latest reporting period, including seven tanker attacks. Five incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz, two in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Three vessels continued their voyages, three required assistance and the outcomes of two remained unknown. None was reported sunk. UKMTO also noted that while most AIS-broadcasting vessels continue to use the Iranian route, more ships are using the southern passage. Most reported projectile strikes since July 6 have occurred along that southern route. More Oil Moving, But Shipping Costs Remain High The recovery in Gulf exports is beginning to ease pressure on global oil markets. According to the IEA, observed oil inventories increased by 52 million barrels in October, while oil volumes on the water jumped by 86 million barrels to their highest level since January. For tanker operators, however, conditions remain difficult. Freight rates for crude shipments from the Middle East to Asia remain near record levels, according to the IEA, even as rates for Aframax and Suezmax tankers have eased. The contrast underscores the uneven recovery. While Gulf producers have restored substantial crude export volumes, commercial shipping continues to operate under significant security constraints. The IEA’s October export figures and UKMTO’s November vessel counts measure different periods and activity, but together point to a market recovering faster than normal shipping conditions. The improvement has also been concentrated in crude oil. Gulf exports of refined products and liquefied petroleum gas remain at roughly half their pre-war levels, contributing to persistent shortages. Diesel is particularly tight, with European prices still near $180 per barrel, roughly 77% above pre-war levels. To ease the shortage, IEA member countries plan to make another 71 million barrels of emergency stocks available by the end of February, including 15 million barrels of diesel. Meanwhile, the recovery in oil supplies has helped push crude prices sharply lower. North Sea Dated crude has fallen from an October peak of $136 per barrel to around $93, although prices remain well above pre-war levels. The latest reports suggest global oil supplies are recovering despite continued disruption to one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. But with tanker attacks continuing, freight rates elevated and Hormuz traffic still far below normal, the recovery remains vulnerable to renewed disruption. articles.title: CMA CGM Demonstrates Relative Resilience in a Volatile Q3
articles.summary: The third quarter of 2026 took place in a volatile economic environment, with persistent tensions in the Middle East impacting international trade and global supply chains. In this context, both shipping and logistics activities were affected…
articles.body: CMA CGM Demonstrates Relative Resilience in a Volatile Q3 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 © Michael Derrer Fuchs - stock.adobe.com The third quarter of 2026 took place in a volatile economic environment, with persistent tensions in the Middle East impacting international trade and global supply chains. In this context, both shipping and logistics activities were affected by adjustments made to trade routes and transport networks. Nevertheless, the global economy demonstrated relative resilience given the scale of the shock to energy prices, while international trade remained dynamic. The Group’s transported volumes increased by 5.5% compared with the third quarter of 2025, outperforming the market. This represents one of the strongest growth rates recorded in recent years. This growth was underpinned by three key drivers: Restocking , as companies sought to build up inventories amid ongoing economic and geopolitical uncertainty; Increased investment in AI-related infrastructure and data centres; Strong momentum in clean technologies and electric vehicles , particularly in China, amid higher hydrocarbon prices. The CMA CGM Group leveraged the complementary strengths of its shipping, logistics and terminal operations to offer customers integrated solutions across the entire supply chain. This strategy is underpinned by investments in port infrastructure, which are essential to expanding the Group’s capacity and strengthening its global network. The Group also accelerated its transformation through innovation and artificial intelligence across all its businesses. MAIA, its agentic AI platform co-developed with Mistral AI, is being progressively rolled out to employees across its shipping, logistics and media businesses. In France, the CMA CGM Group confirms its long-term commitment and contribution to the country's economic, maritime and logistics development. The Group supports 96,500 jobs, including 19,100 direct jobs and 77,400 jobs across the wider economy. The Group has welcomed the first vessels in its new series of 24,000-TEU containerships, including the CMA CGM NOTRE DAME, CMA CGM PANTHEON and CMA CGM ORSAY, which are deployed on its flagship FAL service connecting Asia and Europe. These are the world's largest LNG-powered containerships operating under the French flag. CMA CGM also accelerated the energy transition in shipping through several major alternative fuel bunkering operations: bioethanol in Brazil, bio-LNG in Rotterdam and a world-record biomethanol bunkering operation in Shanghai. CEVA Logistics expanded its international footprint through the acquisition of FedEx Supply Chain and initiated a simplification of its organizational structure under the leadership of Patrick Moebel, aimed at improving its efficiency and strengthening customer proximity CMA CGM further developed its global terminal network, notably through Terminal 4 at the Port of Jeddah in partnership with Red Sea Gateway Terminal, and CMA Terminals' acquisition of a 49% stake in Nador Container Terminal in Morocco. CMA CGM AIR CARGO strengthened its operations during the quarter, with a fleet of eight aircraft now operating under the CMA CGM AIR CARGO and Air Belgium brands, supported by hubs in France, Belgium and the United States. CMA Media launched CMA Sport, while BFMTV maintained its position as France's leading news channel throughout the quarter. Outlook Demand for maritime transport benefited from a strong increase in volumes carried, a trend that is expected to continue over the coming months. Freight rates, which have been rising since the second quarter of 2026, are also supporting the growth of the business. However, the outlook for the coming months remains uncertain. Tensions in the Middle East continue to disrupt shipping routes and weigh on operating costs, while changes in trade policies will continue to influence international trade flows. Against this backdrop, the CMA CGM Group maintains a prudent and responsive approach to management. Its presence across the entire logistics chain, the flexibility of its network and the strength of its balance sheet are major assets in order to cope with changes in its operating environment and provide long-term support to its customers.

articles.title: World Oil Market is Returning to Surplus as Gulf Exports Recover
articles.summary: The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping.

REUTERS/Mohammed Aty LONDON, Nov 13 – The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, the Paris-based agency, which advises industrialized countries, said in a monthly report, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. “The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the agency said in the report. Oil prices reversed earlier gains after the IEA report was released at 0900 GMT. Brent crude LCOc1 was last down 0.1% at $95.71 a barrel. The report follows signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack. The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million bpd of crude in October, OPEC said on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd from September and 97% of the pre-war February volume. OTHER ANALYSTS SEE SIGNS OF SURPLUS Other analysts have also forecast a return to excess supply, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war and continuing tanker attacks in the Gulf. JPMorgan last week forecast a global surplus of 1.4 million bpd in October. High oil prices have also curbed demand this year, helping tip the balance into a surplus. World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.7 million bpd in 2026 to 102.3 million bpd before rebounding by 2 million bpd in 2027, the IEA said, little changed from its previous forecasts. As well as rising output from OPEC+, the IEA flagged supply rising from outside the group. Production from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana will rise by 1.6 million bpd this year, the IEA said. In 2027, global supply is projected to rise by 6.6 million bpd to 108.1 million bpd, led by a further recovery in Gulf output. Still, the 2027 supply growth forecast is down 1.1 million bpd from last month’s report, and the lower outlook partly reflects a downward revision from Iran, the IEA said. Iran is subject to a US blockade that has curbed its oil exports. For 2027, the IEA sees the supply surplus at about 3.8 million bpd, slightly down from a 3.94 million bpd surplus last month. articles.title: CMA CGM Net Profit More Than Triples to $2.32 Billion as Freight Rates Surge
articles.summary: French shipping giant CMA CGM more than tripled its third-quarter net profit as higher container freight rates and strong cargo volumes boosted earnings amid ongoing disruptions to global shipping routes...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy CMA CGM French shipping giant CMA CGM more than tripled its third-quarter net profit as higher container freight rates and strong cargo volumes boosted earnings amid ongoing disruptions to global shipping routes in the Middle East. The Marseille-based group reported Friday that net income attributable to the group climbed to $2.32 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up from $760 million a year earlier, an increase of approximately 205%. Revenue rose 31.1% to $18.4 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) jumped 61.6% to $4.78 billion. The group’s EBITDA margin improved to 25.9%, compared with 21% in the same period last year. The strong results were driven primarily by CMA CGM’s container shipping business, which benefited from sustained demand and elevated freight rates as Middle East tensions continued to disrupt maritime trade routes and global supply chains. CMA CGM carried 6.5 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) during the quarter, up 5.5% year-over-year, outperforming the broader market. Shipping revenue surged 37.3% to $12.3 billion, supported by a 30% increase in average revenue per container to $1,891 per TEU. The division generated $4 billion in EBITDA, compared with $2.2 billion a year earlier, lifting its EBITDA margin to 32.4%. The figures underscore how ongoing disruptions in the Middle East are reshaping the container shipping market, supporting freight rates even as carriers face longer voyages, higher operating costs and changes to established trade routes. “In an uncertain geopolitical environment, the Group has delivered a strong performance in the third quarter,” said Rodolphe Saadé, chairman and CEO of CMA CGM. Saadé pointed to growing shipping volumes, positive results from the company’s terminals business and expansion across air freight and logistics as evidence of the group’s ability to adapt to changing market conditions. CMA CGM said global trade remained resilient despite the geopolitical uncertainty and higher energy prices. The company attributed demand growth partly to businesses rebuilding inventories, increased investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers, and strong demand for clean technologies and electric vehicles, particularly in China. Outside container shipping, the group’s logistics business reported revenue of $5.46 billion, up 19.2% from a year earlier. However, EBITDA declined 14.4% to $366 million, reflecting difficult conditions in freight forwarding and continued weakness in the automotive sector. The company also continued investing in its fleet and global port infrastructure. During the quarter, CMA CGM welcomed the first ships in a new series of 24,000-TEU LNG-powered containerships, including the CMA CGM NOTRE DAME , CMA CGM PANTHEON and CMA CGM ORSAY . The vessels are deployed on the company’s flagship Asia-Europe FAL service and rank among the world’s largest LNG-powered containerships. CMA CGM also expanded its terminal network through a partnership involving Terminal 4 at Saudi Arabia’s Port of Jeddah and the acquisition of a 49% stake in Morocco’s Nador Container Terminal. Looking ahead, CMA CGM expects strong container shipping demand to continue over the coming months , with freight rates that have been rising since the second quarter supporting the business. However, the company warned that the outlook remains uncertain as geopolitical tensions, changing trade policies and disruptions to shipping routes continue to affect global cargo flows. “Tensions in the Middle East continue to disrupt shipping routes and weigh on operating costs,” CMA CGM said in its outlook. The company said its diversified operations, flexible shipping network and strong balance sheet would help it navigate the uncertain trading environment. articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd Profit Surges as Freight Rates Rise, Red Sea Services Return
articles.summary: German container shipping giant Hapag-Lloyd reported a sharp increase in third-quarter earnings as higher freight rates more than offset rising operating costs tied to the Middle East conflict and widespread...

Join the leading maritime news network A hapag-lloyd ship at dock German container shipping giant Hapag-Lloyd reported a sharp increase in third-quarter earnings as higher freight rates more than offset rising operating costs tied to the Middle East conflict and widespread port congestion. The Hamburg-based carrier reported Thursday that third-quarter net profit jumped to $999 million, up from $172 million a year earlier, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) nearly doubled to $1.73 billion. Revenue climbed 26% to $6.88 billion, driven largely by stronger freight rates and high vessel utilization across its global container network. The company’s average freight rate increased 28% to $1,808 per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU), compared with $1,413 in the third quarter of 2025. Transport volumes remained essentially flat at 3.38 million TEU, reflecting continued operational disruptions and capacity constraints. Hapag-Lloyd said the Middle East conflict and congestion at major ports continued to push up operating costs, but higher rates and efficiency improvements more than offset those pressures. “We delivered a strong third quarter, driven by significantly higher spot rates, robust demand and high capacity utilization,” said CEO Rolf Habben Jansen. Operating profit (EBIT) surged to $1.09 billion from $228 million a year earlier. The strong results prompted Hapag-Lloyd to raise its full-year earnings guidance for the third time this year. The company now expects EBITDA of $4.6 billion to $5.0 billion, up from its previous forecast of $3.9 billion to $4.4 billion. Its operating profit forecast was also raised to between $2.0 billion and $2.4 billion, compared with an earlier range of $1.25 billion to $1.75 billion. Red Sea Services Gradually Return The earnings announcement comes as Hapag-Lloyd and its Gemini Cooperation partner Maersk continue gradually restoring container services through the Red Sea and Suez Canal after extended diversions around Africa. In its third-quarter investor presentation , Hapag-Lloyd highlighted the phased return to the shorter Suez route, which it said would reduce transit times, improve Mediterranean connectivity and strengthen schedule reliability. The carrier identified several Asia-Europe services now routed through Suez, including five Far East–South Europe services, one Far East–North Europe service and two India–Europe connections. Other northern European services continue to use the Cape of Good Hope route. Earlier this month, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced that their joint ME1 India–Europe service, known as IOS at Hapag-Lloyd, would switch from the Cape of Good Hope to the Suez Canal. The first westbound departure was scheduled from Salalah on November 4, with the first eastbound departure from Tangier scheduled for November 12–13. The partners have emphasized that further routing decisions remain dependent on security conditions in the Red Sea. The return to Suez could have broader implications for global container shipping capacity. Shorter voyages reduce the number of vessels needed to maintain regular services, potentially releasing capacity that had been tied up in longer diversions around southern Africa. For now, however, Hapag-Lloyd continues to benefit from tight capacity and elevated freight rates. Terminals Business Expands Hapag-Lloyd’s terminal operations also contributed to the improved results. Revenue from its Terminal & Infrastructure segment rose to $197 million from $131 million a year earlier, supported by investments in terminal capacity and improved performance in Latin America and India. The segment’s EBITDA increased to $56 million from $30 million. Despite the strong third quarter, Hapag-Lloyd’s net profit for the first nine months of 2026 was $827 million, down from $946 million in the same period last year, reflecting weaker profitability earlier in the year. The carrier said fourth-quarter performance was developing better than previously expected, supported by continued strong spot freight rates. (File photo: Ken Lund/Wikimedia Commons) A Singapore-flagged bulk carrier struck the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge on the Delaware River Thursday afternoon, leaving the movable span temporarily unable to close and prompting a U.S. Coast Guard inspection of the vessel. The incident occurred around 1:15 p.m. as the 591-foot (180-meter) Strategic Alliance was transiting the river with the bridge’s draw span open for marine traffic, according to the Coast Guard. The vessel, identified in shipping databases as a roughly 40,000-dwt bulk carrier (IMO 9648075), was subsequently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where Coast Guard inspectors were dispatched to assess its condition. No injuries were reported. The circumstances of the collision remain unclear, including which part of the bridge the vessel struck and whether the ship sustained any damage. Authorities have not disclosed what cargo the vessel was carrying or identified a cause for the incident. The bridge, which connects Philadelphia with Palmyra, New Jersey, initially remained in the raised position following the strike. Pennsylvania state Rep. Ed Neilson reported that the bridge was unable to close, triggering major traffic disruptions on both sides of the Delaware River. According to the Associated Press , the Coast Guard said the bridge also remained open to allow another vessel to pass through before the span was eventually lowered. The Burlington County Bridge Commission, which operates the crossing, began inspecting the structure and assessing the extent of the damage. The Tacony-Palmyra Bridge, opened in 1929, spans a navigable section of the Delaware River used by commercial vessels serving terminals upriver from Philadelphia. Its movable span allows larger ships to pass through the crossing. The incident comes amid heightened scrutiny of vessel collision risks at U.S. bridges following the March 2024 collapse of Baltimore’s Francis Scott Key Bridge, which killed six workers after being struck by the containership Dali . In March 2025, the National Transportation Safety Board identified 68 bridges across 19 states requiring vulnerability assessments, warning that the Baltimore bridge’s risk of collapse from a vessel strike had been nearly 30 times the acceptable threshold for critical bridges. The findings raised broader concerns about whether aging bridge infrastructure is adequately protected against collisions with large commercial vessels. The cause of the incident remains under investigation. Authorities have not reported whether the collision resulted in any restrictions on commercial vessel movements along the Delaware River. articles.title: ADNOC L&S reports sharp profit growth and raises 2026 outlook
articles.summary: ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADNOC L&S) reported a sharp increase in third-quarter earnings, supported by higher global shipping rates and strong demand for energy transportation. The Abu Dhabi-based company recorded a net profit of US$887 million in the third quarter of 2026, up 321% from US$211 million a year...
articles.body: ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADNOC L&S) reported a sharp increase in third-quarter earnings, supported by higher global shipping rates and strong demand for energy transportation. The Abu Dhabi-based company recorded a net profit of US$887 million in the third quarter of 2026, up 321% from US$211 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, revenue increased by 149% to US$3.29 billion. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose by 187% to US$1.09 billion. The performance reflected stronger shipping market conditions and contributions from the company’s expanding fleet. For the first nine months of 2026, ADNOC L&S reported revenue of US$6.96 billion, representing an 82% year-on-year increase. Net profit climbed by 227% to US$2.06 billion, while EBITDA reached US$2.56 billion. Shipping business drives earnings growth The Shipping segment delivered the strongest performance during the nine-month period. Revenue increased by 217% to US$5.09 billion, while EBITDA rose by 362% to US$2.02 billion. Furthermore, the segment’s net profit reached US$1.77 billion, representing an 846% increase compared with the same period in 2025. According to the company, higher global charter rates supported the results. Additional contributions came from chartering activities and vessels delivered during 2026 and the final quarter of 2025. However, performance across the company’s other business segments was mixed. Integrated Logistics revenue declined by 19% to US$1.59 billion, following the completion of the Al Omairah Island project in late 2025. The segment’s EBITDA also fell by 29% to US$448 million. Regional geopolitical conditions affected the utilisation and charter rates of the company’s jack-up barge fleet. Higher operating costs added further pressure on earnings. In contrast, the Services segment recorded revenue growth of 5% to US$281 million. EBITDA increased by 76% to US$90 million, supported by commercial pooling activities and stronger bunkering margins at Integr8. ADNOC L&S upgrades full-year guidance Following the strong performance, ADNOC L&S raised its earnings guidance for 2026 for the fourth time this year. The company now expects full-year net profit of approximately US$4 billion. Its revised outlook reflects stronger shipping market conditions and the earnings recorded through October. ADNOC L&S also expects revenue growth in the low 100% range and EBITDA growth in the low 210% range for the full year. These estimates represent substantial increases compared with its previous guidance. Nevertheless, the company said its full-year performance remains sensitive to regional developments and changing market conditions. “Resilience has defined our performance this year, reflecting the strength of our people and our businesses. Our seafarers and employees continue to deliver energy from the UAE to the world, while our global platform and long-term contracts are generating significant value and returns for our shareholders,” said Captain Abdulkareem Al Masabi, CEO, ADNOC L&S. The company has committed US$7 billion in capital expenditure through 2030 as it continues to expand its maritime and logistics operations. Meanwhile, its board approved an interim cash dividend of US$85.3 million for the third quarter of 2026. The company also maintained its policy of increasing annual dividends per share by at least 5% through 2030.

articles.summary: Russia’s October revenues from crude and petroleum-product exports hit the highest since May as the ongoing Iran war bolstered oil prices, according to the International Energy Agency.

REUTERS/Anton Vaganov/File Photo By Bloomberg News Nov 13, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Russia’s October revenues from crude and petroleum-product exports hit the highest since May as the ongoing Iran war bolstered oil prices, according to the International Energy Agency. Russian oil producers earned almost $21.2 billion in export revenue last month, up about 65% from a year earlier, the IEA said in a report Friday. Crude accounted for more than 80% of the total, as the nation’s petroleum-product output and exports were pressured by Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries. The country’s key crude blends, Urals and ESPO, topped $100 a barrel last month due to hostilities in the Middle East, with near daily attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and intense strikes by Houthis on Saudi energy infrastructure, the agency said. That supported demand for Russian barrels, which don’t need to cross Hormuz to reach China and India, their main buyers. Prices above $100 were a welcome development for Russia’s budget, which gets about a fifth of its revenue from the oil and gas industry and which has been strained by the cost of the invasion of Ukraine and sustaining the nation’s wartime economy. The full-year budget deficit is expected to reach 3.2% of gross domestic product this year, government data published Tuesday show. The federal budget doesn’t receive oil revenues directly from exports, but rather through taxing producers, while offering generous subsidies to the industry at the same time. Last month, net budget revenues from oil levies totaled around $10 billion, dented by multi-billion-ruble payouts to support domestic fuel deliveries, Bloomberg calculations based on Finance Ministry data show. Read More: Russia Refinery Payouts Hit Highest Since 2022 in Blow to Budget Russia’s crude oil exports in October remained flat month-on-month at 5.33 million barrels per day, roughly 4% above last year’s level, according to the IEA report. Petroleum-product exports reached 1.49 million barrels per day, the highest since June, though were about a third below the year-earlier level. Ukrainian drone attacks in the first half of October impacted Russian refinery runs, before easing later in the month as Kyiv paused strikes for two weeks. The lull coincided with calls for calm from US President Donald Trump as he sought to bring down fuel prices before the midterm elections. Ukraine has since resumed targeting some of Russia’s key oil refineries, including export-focused plants as Kirishi, and the nation’s largest facility in Omsk. The renewed campaign has already hurt Russian refinery runs, and may lead to higher seaborne crude exports this month, unless Russia’s crude-export terminals are affected. Singapore also maintained its leading position in three of the five pillars* assessed in the report — Shipping, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness. These complementary strengths provide maritime companies with access to markets, business opportunities and specialized expertise, making Singapore an attractive location for companies to establish their presence and grow their businesses. This ecosystem is supported by Singapore’s position as one of the world’s busiest ports, connected to more than 600 ports worldwide. In 2025, the Port of Singapore handled a record 44.66 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in container throughput and 3.22 billion gross tonnage in vessel arrival. Singapore also remained the world’s largest bunkering port, with marine fuel sales reaching a record 56.77 million tonnes. Continued investments in port automation, maritime digitalization, innovation and the adoption of alternative marine fuels further strengthen the ecosystem and create new opportunities for maritime businesses. articles.body: Italian shipbuilding group Fincantieri reported higher profitability in the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger operating margins and continued demand across its main markets. The company also raised its full-year earnings guidance as its order backlog reached a new record. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased by 10.9% to €511 million, compared with €461 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, the EBITDA margin improved to 7.7%, up from 6.9% in the same period of 2025. However, revenue declined slightly to €6.61 billion from €6.73 billion last year. According to Fincantieri, growth in its commercial businesses and Underwater division partly offset changes in defence programmes and the impact of a major Indonesian naval order recorded in 2025. The company also strengthened its financial position. Adjusted net debt decreased to €730 million at the end of September, compared with €1.31 billion at the end of 2025. The improvement reflected cash generation and a capital increase completed in February. Shipbuilding backlog reaches record levels Fincantieri’s confirmed order backlog reached €44.7 billion, representing an 8.8% increase from the end of 2025. Its total backlog, including additional commercial commitments, rose by 14.9% to €72.6 billion. The company secured €9.7 billion in new orders during the first nine months of 2026. This represents approximately 88% of its annual order intake target of around €11 billion. In addition, Fincantieri signed contracts worth €12.3 billion that had not yet become effective by 30 September. These agreements were therefore excluded from the reported order intake. During the reporting period, the shipbuilder delivered 19 vessels from ten shipyards. Its order book included 90 vessels, with scheduled deliveries extending through 2036. The delivery horizon could extend to 2039 when including a Princess Cruises order signed in April 2026, which remains subject to financing. Fincantieri also highlighted a contract for two DDX destroyers for the Italian Navy. The agreement represents approximately €1.8 billion for the company, including €800 million in options. articles.body: The DynaLiners Shares Index (DLSI) recorded its fourth consecutive weekly decline, falling by 111 points, or 4.1%, to 2,583, as losses spread across the maritime and container shipping sectors. According to DynaLiners, all sector indices finished the week lower, with the sharpest decline recorded by DLSI Carriers, which lost 239 points, equivalent to a 6% contraction. The latest figures extend a month-long downward trend in shipping-related equities, with container carriers experiencing particularly strong selling pressure. Declines outnumber gains across shipping stocks Negative performance was widespread among the companies tracked by the index, with 67 recording share-price declines compared with 53 that registered gains. The average share-price movement across the companies covered was a loss of 1.1%. Among the strongest performers, Vietnam’s An Giang Port led the gains with a 17% increase, closely followed by shipowner Seacon Shipping, whose shares advanced by 16%. Only one other company recorded an increase exceeding 10%. At the opposite end, Regional Container Lines (RCL) and Salalah Port registered the largest declines, with both companies losing 18% of their share value. Another six companies experienced share-price reductions of at least 10%, highlighting the extent of the downward pressure across the sector. The fourth consecutive weekly decline also raises questions about the divergence between investor sentiment and the earnings expectations of shipping companies. DynaLiners questioned whether carriers may have been too optimistic in their recent upward revisions to full-year expectations, particularly given the sustained weakness in shipping-related equities. However, stock market performance alone does not establish whether those financial projections will be achieved, with future earnings also dependent on freight market conditions, operating costs and developments in global trade.

articles.body: Singapore-Registered Bulk Carrier Strikes US Bridge, Disrupts Traffic Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 The Tacony-Palmyra Bridge spanning the Delaware River between Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and Palmyra, New Jersey, pictured in June 2010 (Credit: Jag9889 / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0) The Singapore-registered bulk carrier STRATEGIC ALLIANCE has struck the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge over the Delaware River between Pennsylvania and New Jersey, forcing a temporary closure before vehicle traffic was partially restored. The incident occurred shortly after 1 p.m. local time on November 12 during a bridge opening for marine traffic, according to the Burlington County Bridge Commission. Representative Ed Neilson reported that the bridge was initially unable to close following the collision, causing significant traffic congestion on the Philadelphia side. The bridge was closed to motorists and pedestrians while officials investigated potential structural damage. Pedestrian access to the bridge remained prohibited. Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) confirmed that STRATEGIC ALLIANCE was involved in the incident, reporting no injuries to civilians or crew members, no major damage to the vessel and no marine pollution. The bulk carrier is safely moored at the Kinder Morgan terminal in Pennsylvania, according to MPA. The Singaporean authority said it was in contact with the vessel's management company and relevant US authorities to establish the circumstances of the incident and would conduct an investigation. Repairs and inspections of the bridge are continuing.

articles.body: Ocean Network Express (ONE) has announced a reduction of approximately 18.2% in its Inland Fuel Charges (IFL/IFD) for carrier haulage operations in Thailand, effective from 20 November 2026. The revised charges will apply to import and export containers moving through Laem Chabang terminals via Bangkok Private Wharfs (BKK) and Lat Krabang (LKR), covering all trade lanes and transportation modes included in the carrier’s inland haulage arrangements. For shipments handled through Bangkok Private Wharfs, the surcharge on 20-foot containers will decrease from THB 330 to THB 270, while the charge for 40-foot containers will fall from THB 660 to THB 540. ONE introduced its inland fuel surcharge arrangements in Thailand earlier this year in response to fuel supply volatility and logistics challenges associated with developments in the Middle East. According to ONE, the surcharge is based on fuel costs and is subject to reviews and possible adjustments every two weeks. articles.title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
articles.summary: Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is...
articles.body: Containers Contributions From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 0 3 minutes read Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. The sinking of the SS United States reminds us that ships can outlive their commercial purpose. Launched in 1951 and entering service in 1952, the SS United States was the pinnacle of post-war American maritime engineering. It held the record as the world’s fastest passenger ship but was withdrawn in 1969 as commercial aviation transformed the economics of transatlantic travel. It was not poor engineering that made the ship obsolete, it was a market that had moved on. After decades moored in Philadelphia, the vessel was acquired by Okaloosa County in a project valued at approximately $13m. Its new role will support tourism, marine conservation and research. Its retirement offers a useful perspective on container shipping as it now faces another turning point. A substantial wave of new capacity The container shipping industry is preparing for a significant increase in fleet capacity. According to Drewry’s third-quarter 2026 Container Forecaster the global containership orderbook stood at approximately 13.9m teu on 1 September 2026, equivalent to 40.9% of the active fleet. Drewry forecasts fleet growth of 8.4% in 2027, rising to 12.1% in 2028 before moderating to 9.4% in 2029. The concern is the market into which these ships will be delivered. During the pandemic, congestion, equipment shortages and route disruption absorbed vessel capacity. Diversions around the Cape of Good Hope lengthened voyages and tied up ships. Carriers responded by ordering larger, more fuel-efficient vessels anticipating continued trade growth, but shipbuilding schedules are long and in the era of the never normal, market conditions change quickly. If Red Sea and Suez Canal routings return progressively to normal, shorter voyages could release significant effective capacity without a single additional ship entering service. Combined with newbuildings, this could widen the gap between supply and demand. Vessel capacity could potentially reach as much as 10% above demand under such circumstances. The consequences could include lower freight rates, tougher competition for cargo, blank sailings, slower steaming, vessel idling and accelerated recycling of older tonnage. The industry faces a major capacity-management challenge. The cost of getting the timing wrong Aviation permanently changed the market for passenger liners, while container shipping remains essential to trade. New vessels will not automatically become redundant. Nevertheless, ships are long-term capital investments, ordered years before delivery and expected to earn returns over operating lives spanning decades. A vessel ordered when freight rates are high and capacity constrained may enter service when demand is weaker, transit times are shorter and competing tonnage is plentiful. Efficiency alone cannot guarantee a satisfactory return. Carriers will have to decide which vessels to deploy, which trades to prioritise and when to redeploy or retire older ships. Smaller vessels displaced from mainline routes may move into regional trades, adding competitive pressure whilst others may be laid up, sold or recycled. Ports and terminals may see service patterns, berth requirements and transhipment flows change. Shippers may welcome lower rates but carriers protecting utilisation may consolidate services, withdraw sailings or alter port rotations. Lower prices could therefore come with less predictable frequency and transit times. The costs of poor capacity planning will ultimately ripple through businesses to end users and consumers. A different future for ageing vessels The SS United States project raises the question of what happens when ships lose their original commercial purpose. Conversion into an artificial reef offers a potential tourism and conservation role but it is neither a universal nor necessarily economical solution for commercial vessels. For surplus container ships, recycling will remain the principal end-of-life option when redeployment is no longer viable. Some older vessels may serve feeder networks or specialised trades, provided their economics remain competitive. Fleet renewal should consider the economic, environmental and operational consequences of retiring existing tonnage and not just the efficiency gains promised by newbuildings. The SS United States was a remarkable engineering achievement but it could not escape changing transportation economics. Its story reminds us that a ship’s commercial lifespan is determined not simply by how well it is built but by whether the market still needs what it does. As the industry approaches 2027, the question is whether carriers have ordered more capacity than the market can sustainably absorb and how prepared they are to manage the consequences. The challenge is not simply to build the next generation of vessels. It is to ensure there is a commercially sustainable reason to put them to work. It’s not something we as an industry have a good track doing. "That means the market is roughly balanced, with the ability to trade up limited and the ability to trade down limited," he said. Oil has had a volatile trading week, with earlier hopes for a rapprochement in the US-Israeli war on Iran, now in its ninth month, offset by strikes on Saudi Arabian infrastructure by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and attacks on tankers shipping crude out of the Gulf. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social a deal with Iran was not necessary to end the war. "Trump's indications that further military escalation against Iran may not be necessary have raised expectations that Washington could increasingly rely on economic sanctions and restrictions on oil shipments rather than intensifying military operations," said Sugandha Sachdeva, founder of SS WealthStreet, a New Delhi-based research firm. The weakness in oil prices is also largely driven by signs of softening US demand, as rising crude oil and fuel inventories indicate a relatively subdued consumption outlook, Sachdeva said. US crude and fuel inventories rose last week, driven by softer refined products demand and a jump in oil imports, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday. Despite the easing prices, risks remain for oil shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway for crude exports from the main Middle East producers. On Thursday, Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian accounts. That same day, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked a pumping station on the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, an oil facility in the Saudi Red Sea city of Yanbu, and an Aramco building in the capital Riyadh. "Geopolitical risks remain elevated, and any fresh disruption to oil supplies could quickly reignite upward pressure on prices," Sachdeva of SS WealthStreet said. articles.body: Environment Middle East Tankers Gulf war leaves toxic legacy that could last decades Sam Chambers November 13, 2026 0 342 2 minutes read CENTCOM CENTCOM Greenpeace has identified 540 possible oil spills across the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran war began on February 28 (see map below), with satellite imagery showing a cumulative slick footprint of approximately 20,000 sq km. Not all detections have been conclusively linked to attacks on shipping. The environmental consequences could last for decades. A 2022 study published in the Journal of Marine Science and Engineering found extensive oil deposits along more than 25 km of Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island coastline, almost 40 years after the 1983–85 Nowruz oil spills during the Iran-Iraq war. Researchers found oil contamination in 76% of 1,434 test pits, demonstrating how petroleum residues can persist long after surface slicks disappear. The spills continue daily with many more strikes on ships being reported every week. Iran has claimed that four oil tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz over the past two days, while a separately confirmed attack on a Sinokor-operated tanker off the United Arab Emirates forced the evacuation of 22 seafarers. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed yesterday that two supertankers carrying more than 4m barrels of oil between them had been disabled by explosions on Wednesday after ignoring warnings against using what Tehran described as an unauthorised route through the strait. Iranian state media attributed the explosions to naval mines and broadcast footage purporting to show the incidents. The Iranian army subsequently claimed that another two tankers struck mines in the eastern part of the strait on Thursday afternoon after ignoring navigation warnings and switching off their radar systems. None of the four vessels has been identified, and the claims have not been independently verified. Separately, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed that a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, at 1800 GMT on Wednesday. The projectile hit the vessel’s engine room, starting a fire and forcing the evacuation of its crew. India’s shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal subsequently identified the vessel as the Liberia-flagged Dominica Prosperity, reporting that all 22 crew members, including 19 Indian nationals, had been safely evacuated. The tanker was drifting off Mina Saqr when the attack occurred. The International Maritime Organization’s latest tally of Hormuz strikes, covering incidents confirmed through November 11, stands at 134, with 25 seafarers killed since the conflict began in late February. articles.title: Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial
articles.summary: One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. The three-week trial ended...
articles.body: Europe Tankers Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial Sam Chambers November 13, 2026 0 325 2 minutes read One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. The three-week trial ended yesterday, with judgment expected to take several months. At the centre of the dispute is TD3C, the Baltic’s benchmark for transporting crude from Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia to Ningbo, China, a voyage requiring passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Mercuria has argued that the disruption following the outbreak of hostilities on February 28 rendered the benchmark unreliable, with insufficient physical tanker activity to support meaningful assessments. The trading house maintains that the Baltic failed to meet its statutory and contractual obligations by continuing to publish rates despite mounting evidence that its contributing shipbrokers could not reliably determine a market price. During the trial, Mercuria highlighted internal communications revealing considerable uncertainty among Baltic staff and broker panellists. One Baltic assessor reportedly described the rates as “utter nonsense”, while a contributing broker questioned how a market could be assessed when virtually no vessels were fixing voyages. Mercuria also challenged the Baltic’s reliance on forward freight agreement prices when calculating a benchmark that itself underpins derivatives contracts, raising concerns about circular pricing. However, the trader significantly narrowed its case during closing arguments, abandoning demands for retrospective invalidation or suspension of the index. The Baltic, owned by the Singapore Exchange, has vigorously rejected the allegations, arguing that its established methodology remained appropriate despite extraordinary market conditions. Its lawyers maintain that experienced shipbrokers could still assess freight values using available market intelligence, including transactions, vessel movements and derivatives pricing. The exchange also pointed to continuing vessel transits through Hormuz during the disputed period, disputing Mercuria’s contention that there was no meaningful underlying market. In closing arguments, the Baltic accused Mercuria of repeatedly changing its case and suggested the litigation was an attempt to escape the consequences of unsuccessful trading positions. Mercuria rejected allegations of wrongdoing. The Baltic has also warned that retrospective intervention in a widely used benchmark could create significant uncertainty for freight derivatives and physical shipping contracts linked to TD3C. The dispute has exposed uncomfortable questions about the governance of shipping’s freight indices, particularly when geopolitical events make conventional market assessments exceptionally difficult. The Baltic Exchange has consistently defended its benchmark procedures and regulatory compliance. Mr Justice Andrew Baker must now determine whether those procedures satisfied the exchange’s obligations during an unprecedented disruption to tanker trading. The implications extend well beyond the two companies, potentially influencing how freight benchmarks are maintained during future market emergencies. articles.title: New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping
articles.summary: Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia...
articles.body: Contributions Greater China New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 933 8 minutes read Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia and chartered from Singapore. Its cargo need never pass through Hong Kong’s harbour. Even its Hong Kong financing vehicle may have to seek credit approval elsewhere. The geography of shipping has always been complicated. What has changed is the urgency with which Hong Kong must ask where the real business takes place. Is the city still a maritime capital in its own right, chosen by international owners, traders and financiers because of what it offers? Or is it becoming a highly sophisticated services counter for the vast industrial and commercial machine next door? On paper, the answer looks reassuring. Hong Kong remains fourth in the 2026 Xinhua-Baltic international maritime centre rankings, behind Singapore, Shanghai and London. Three of the world’s leading shipmanagement companies are headquartered here, major P&I clubs operate here, and the city retains a formidable concentration of lawyers, financiers and technical expertise. Look towards the waterfront, however, and a different picture emerges. The container port handled 12.99m teu in 2025, scarcely half its 2008 peak. The register has shed substantial tonnage amid geopolitical upheaval, falling to 109m gt by June this year. Shanghai, Shenzhen and Guangzhou have grown into maritime giants whose physical advantages Hong Kong cannot realistically overturn. These are not contradictory stories. Together they define the central question running through this special report: whether Hong Kong can convert its inherited maritime strengths into a sustainable business model for 2030, even as its traditional measures of importance become less flattering. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, resists the suggestion that the city is being reduced to an adjunct of the mainland. “An ‘annex’ does not host three of the world’s top 10 shipmanagers, 11 of the 12 International Group P&I associations, eight of the top ten ship-finance bookrunners,” he says, pointing also to the city’s legal institutions and international industry organisations. This inventory represents decades of investment and commercial trust. Yet it does not settle the more difficult question of what those institutions actually do here, or whether their next expansion will take place somewhere else. Where the decisions are made Hong Kong has spent much of this decade making itself more attractive on tax. Qualifying ship lessors can enjoy a zero profits-tax rate; eligible ship leasing managers, shipmanagers, agents and brokers benefit from half-rate treatment, as do certain marine insurers. The administration has also sought to broaden the proposition to physical commodity traders, recognising that traders create demand for chartering, insurance, finance and legal services The first results are tangible, but open to interpretation. Government figures show the number of ship leasing enterprises under the relevant preferential regime rising from 11 in 2020/21 to 46 in 2022/23. That is evidence that structures and businesses have responded. It says much less about the location of credit committees, the people selecting vessels or the teams negotiating charters. “Tax is necessary but not sufficient,” Hext says. Companies, he argues, follow customers, skills, capital and regulatory certainty. He wants the next phase judged by “regional headquarters, underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks and skilled jobs, and not by company registrations alone”. Gautam Chellaram, chairman of KC Maritime, is more sceptical about what tax reform has delivered. He sees genuine growth in leasing and mainland-linked finance, but says: “I do not yet see clear evidence that the measures have resulted in substantial headquarters relocation involving decision-makers, fund managers, and independent shipowners physically basing themselves in Hong Kong.” It would be equally wrong to dismiss the developments as bookkeeping. Hong Kong is a place where ships are managed, risks assessed and capital arranged, not merely where documents are signed. Dockendale Group is among the companies expanding management operations locally. Its chief executive, Vikrant Gusain, says Hong Kong’s ease of doing business is an important factor in the decision, alongside access to Asian markets and international talent. The competitive comparison nevertheless remains Singapore. “Singapore continues to offer broader tax incentives and a larger concentration of commodity traders,” says Jim James, senior consultant at Hill Dickinson. The latter point may be more important than the former. Traders and charterers bring transactions, and transactions bring the brokers, lenders, insurers and lawyers who serve them. A critical mass of principals is extraordinarily difficult to manufacture through concessions alone. Hong Kong has distinct advantages of its own. Its banking network connects Chinese and international capital; its offshore renminbi role creates opportunities for trade and leasing; and its links with a vast manufacturing and shipbuilding hinterland provide access that a competing maritime centre cannot reproduce. But geographical proximity is not the same thing as commercial gravity. The city must persuade companies to put people with mandates and budgets here, not just a local subsidiary. June’s tax amendment bill, including a proposed half-rate concession for qualifying physical commodity trading, gives the policy another push. September’s first five-year plan adds a ‘Finance + Maritime’ agenda built around ship finance, insurance, trade finance and related services. Neither initiative can be called successful solely because it exists. Their test will be new trading desks, lending decisions and customers with genuine freedom to transact elsewhere. The mainland advantage — and the danger Where does this leave the argument that Hong Kong is becoming Shanghai’s professional-services annex? Chellaram offers the report’s most uncomfortable formulation: as a cargo port, the city is being functionally subordinated to mainland competitors, but as a financial, legal and arbitration centre it retains qualities not available in the same combination across the border. “On the professional-services side, Hong Kong is the piece Shanghai structurally cannot replicate,” he says. The separate customs territory, common-law system, freely convertible currency and established international business practices all give the city a distinctive purpose. The opportunity is to sell those qualities to the world, not simply to companies moving through China. Damien Laracy, partner and head of Hill Dickinson’s Hong Kong office, describes a transition “from a cargo-driven port hub to a specialised centre for maritime services”. Rather than an annex, he sees “the region’s high-value maritime services platform, complementing the manufacturing, cargo, and port capacity of neighbouring cities”. The distinction is subtle but critical. A law firm advising a mainland shipowner on a vessel financing can be doing genuine international business from Hong Kong. So can an insurer handling a casualty thousands of miles away or a manager overseeing a fleet trading between Brazil and India. But the city’s position becomes more vulnerable if its principal attraction is merely that it makes mainland transactions easier. The international test is whether owners and counterparties with no direct mainland connection still choose Hong Kong. The machinery of a genuine maritime centre is already here. English-language maritime contracts, established common-law precedents, internationally recognised arbitration and access to mainland enforcement arrangements give it a credible offering. Rosita Lau, a partner at Ince, is among those urging the city to promote its legal and dispute-resolution capabilities far more systematically. The fact that Hong Kong can be chosen in a contract is not proof that it will be. There are also more prosaic measures of legal competitiveness. Martyn Huckerby, head of competition law and regulatory at Hill Dickinson, points to the extension of the block exemption for liner vessel-sharing agreements to 2031. The renewal, he says, preserves “legal certainty for operational cooperation between liner shipping companies”. It is a narrow regulatory decision, but one of the many predictable rules on which internationally mobile businesses build long-term operations. Insurance offers another illustration of integration without inevitable subordination. London P&I has served shipowners from Hong Kong for decades and opened an office in Shanghai in 2025. Deborah Yu, its regional director for Asia, says the two offices work together with the club’s operations in London and Athens. The point is not to force every Asian insurance decision into Hong Kong, but to ensure the city continues to handle work that could plausibly be located elsewhere. International outlook An international city must keep choosing to be international. That means foreign owners can operate comfortably, specialist staff can build careers and global counterparties can trust their contracts, information and capital to an environment they understand. This issue explores what that requirement means in practice. Hong Kong’s shipmanagement concentration provides a genuine strategic asset: it would take years to reproduce the crewing, technical and training networks that leading managers have built here. The challenge is keeping enough experienced people to make decisions locally as digitalisation, alternative fuels and increasingly complex compliance change the skill set. The same logic applies to finance and insurance. An internationally recognised logo on a Hong Kong office does not tell us whether it can approve a ship loan or underwrite a specialist risk. A registry’s gross tonnage does not establish where the family that owns the ship runs its business. A port’s box count says little about the value of transactions governed by local law, but the loss of container activity cannot be waved away simply by relabelling the city a services centre. Technology adds a further test. Hong Kong’s Port Community System is meant to help connect cargo movements, documentation and financing across the supply chain. But common platforms are only as useful as the trust and security behind them. Paul Haswell, technology partner at Hill Dickinson, notes that digitisation will bring “increased emphasis on data security and the monitoring of systems”. A financial and logistics crossroads cannot afford to treat cyber resilience as an optional extra. The city’s new maritime ambitions, particularly green bunkering and transition finance, depend on the same mixture of hard infrastructure and intangible trust. There is little value in promoting alternative fuels unless ships can take them safely, on schedule and at competitive prices. There is little point marketing green ship finance unless lenders and owners are prepared to commit capital against realistic assumptions about technology, fuel availability and earnings. Government has clearly recognised the need to change. Its first five-year plan shifts the emphasis from volume to value, promising stronger maritime services, a greener and smarter port, closer links with the Greater Bay Area and a more developed marine finance ecosystem. The question is no longer whether officials have ambitions. It is whether businesses can see projects proceeding quickly enough, and with sufficient commercial substance, to justify staying and expanding. That demands a sharper understanding of competition. Singapore can be a partner and a rival. Shanghai can be a customer, collaborator and competitor. The Greater Bay Area can supply Hong Kong with enormous commercial opportunities while simultaneously taking cargo, talent and investment from it. Those apparently inconsistent propositions are the reality of a maritime industry in which business moves wherever the overall proposition is strongest. The defensible future is neither a nostalgic campaign to win back every container nor a comfortable acceptance of being the mainland’s legal and financial back office. It is a city that remains indispensable to international shipping because substantive work is done there: ships are managed, cargo is traded, capital is committed, risks are insured and disputes are resolved. By 2030, Hong Kong should be judged less by how many companies have an address in Central or how many development plans have been published, and more by who has authority to do business from the city. Are the next fleet acquisitions decided here? Are traders locating profitable operations here? Are international parties choosing Hong Kong law when they have no obligation to do so? Are young maritime professionals staying because the best opportunities are available here? A gateway is somewhere business passes through. A maritime capital is somewhere business chooses to stay. Hong Kong has spent generations proving it can be both. The coming four years will show whether it still can. You can read the magazine ahead of Hong Kong Maritime Week by clicking here . Our opening week highlighted some uncomfortable realities. Tanker masters are earning less in real terms than they were 16 years ago , despite the extraordinary freight boom, while a Splash Crew investigation found that at least 69 merchant seafarers have been killed in war-related attacks this year , a death toll not seen since the tanker wars of the 1980s. Elsewhere, China is facing a growing shortage of junior officers , the family of a Finnish seafarer jailed in Turkey made an urgent appeal for medical intervention , and the secretary-general of InterManager examined how rest hour records can bear little resemblance to life at sea in an exclusive article for Splash Crew. There was some potential good news for overworked crews, however, with maritime technology executives predicting that AI could consign the traditional noon report and much of shipping’s paperwork mountain to history . The wars themselves showed no sign of abating. Greenpeace has identified 540 possible oil spills since the US-Iran conflict began in February, with research suggesting the environmental damage could persist for decades. In the Baltic, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian export port of Ust-Luga , setting fire to infrastructure and disrupting power supplies. In our latest Maritime CEO interview, MSM boss Faouzi Fradi argued that shipmanagement’s next competitive advantage will be trust rather than size. Technology featured prominently elsewhere. A global Microsoft outage exposed shipping’s growing dependence on a handful of tech giants, while SplashTech asked whether maritime AI has already become a commodity , with industry leaders arguing that proprietary data and maritime expertise, rather than the AI models themselves, will increasingly separate winners from losers. Over at Splash Ports , MSC chief executive Soren Toft warned that port congestion has become a new normal , with millions of teu of capacity tied up in delays. Splash Cruise , meanwhile, caught up with expedition veteran Jan Bryde , who, after 33 trips to the North Pole, is turning his attention to Europe’s rivers. Finally, this week’s Splash Wrap podcast, carried below, examines the extraordinary legal showdown between the Baltic Exchange and Mercuria. The three-week London trial has concluded, with a verdict expected in the coming months on whether the world’s leading VLCC freight benchmark remained fit for purpose after war erupted in the Middle East. articles.summary: The SS United States has settled upright on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico, completing its transformation from record-breaking ocean liner to the world’s largest artificial reef. Early sonar...
