Join the leading maritime news network Image courtesy SS United States: An Operational Guide to America's Flagship The SS United States has settled upright on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico, completing its transformation from record-breaking ocean liner to the world’s largest artificial reef. Early sonar and remotely operated vehicle inspections confirmed that the 990-foot vessel came to rest upright, just feet from its intended location, following its controlled sinking off Florida’s Gulf Coast on Wednesday, November 11. The first underwater images are also emerging. RV Explorer, a shipwreck research and salvage vessel based in Cape May, New Jersey, shared an image of diver Captain Will Hinton positioned in front of the ship’s stern. “Happy to report the SS United States is sitting perfectly upright,” RV Explorer said. The confirmation marks a significant milestone for a project that required extensive preparation to ensure the historic vessel would settle safely on the seabed and remain accessible to divers. According to Destin-Fort Walton Beach tourism officials, the ship now rests approximately 22 nautical miles offshore in about 180 feet of water, with its uppermost deck roughly 60 feet below the surface. The safety zone surrounding the deployment site has been lifted, allowing divers to begin exploring the wreck. “The successful deployment of the SS United States is a significant achievement, and I couldn’t be prouder of the team,” said Jennifer Adams, tourism director for Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “To see a vessel of this size come to rest upright, within feet of its intended location, is a great testament to the expertise and collaboration of everyone who helped bring this ambitious vision to life.” The SS United States was deliberately sunk on Veterans Day after weather concerns prompted Okaloosa County to move the operation forward from its original November 12 schedule. Hundreds of spectators gathered aboard nearby boats to witness the final moments of the ship that once held the title of the world’s fastest ocean liner. Crews opened intake valves to allow Gulf waters to flood the vessel in a controlled sinking operation. The ship gradually submerged before rolling to port and sinking below the surface, eventually settling onto the seabed. The deployment followed extensive work to prepare the former passenger liner for its new role, including environmental remediation and structural modifications designed to make the wreck safer for divers and marine life. The SS United States joins more than 580 artificial reef sites in the Destin-Fort Walton Beach area, although none comes close to matching its scale. “This sets Okaloosa County apart as a leader in the tourism industry worldwide and we could not be happier to see this project come to fruition,” said Okaloosa County Board Chairman Trey Goodwin. Beyond its significance as a diving attraction, the ship will become a large-scale marine research site. Scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Dauphin Island Sea Lab and Louisiana State University will monitor biological, physical and chemical changes around the vessel as marine organisms begin colonizing its structure. Researchers hope the project will provide new insights into how artificial reefs develop over time and support marine ecosystems. “This is so much more than creating a new dive destination,” said Alex Fogg, natural resources chief for Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before.” For the SS United States , the deployment marks another chapter in a remarkable history. Built in Newport News, Virginia, the liner entered service in 1952 and set a transatlantic speed record on her maiden voyage that remains unbeaten by any ocean liner. After retiring in 1969, she spent decades laid up, including a long period on the Philadelphia waterfront, as preservation efforts struggled to secure her future. Now, the former flagship has a permanent home beneath the Gulf. A future shoreside museum and visitor experience, being developed with the SS United States Conservancy, will preserve the ship’s history and artifacts for visitors who may never venture underwater. “Her legacy will live on,” said Conservancy Board Chair Susan Gibbs. The artificial reef project was funded through tourism revenue and contributions from project partners. articles.summary: By Lori-Ann LaRocco The Port of Los Angeles handled a record 1,026,872 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, marking its second-busiest month ever and extending the strongest five-month cargo run...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. By Lori-Ann LaRocco The Port of Los Angeles handled a record 1,026,872 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, marking its second-busiest month ever and extending the strongest five-month cargo run in the port’s 118-year history. The October total followed September’s all-time record of 1,042,652 TEUs, marking the first time the nation’s busiest container port has surpassed 1 million units in consecutive months. Los Angeles has now crossed that threshold three times in 2026, another first. “On the heels of September’s all-time record, October makes it our second-best month ever,” said Port Executive Director Gene Seroka during a media briefing. “No other U.S. port has handled 1 million units in a single month, and we’ve now done it three times this year, including back-to-back months for the first time ever.” From June through October, the port processed nearly 5 million TEUs, its strongest five-month stretch on record. “What’s remarkable isn’t just the record volume but our ability to sustain this level of activity month after month,” Seroka said in a statement Thursday. Seroka attributed the historic cargo activity to continued consumer spending, retailers replenishing inventories, changes in trade policy and disruptions along other global shipping routes. Loaded imports reached 538,620 TEUs in October, up 25% from a year earlier and 30% above the port’s five-year October average. “This strength goes beyond holiday merchandise,” Seroka said. “We’re moving consumer goods alongside parts, components, and equipment destined for American businesses and manufacturers across the country.” The port also handled a record 373,271 empty TEUs, surpassing the previous monthly record set in September. Ocean carriers have been repositioning equipment to Asia to accommodate additional shipments. Exports, however, remain a weak spot. Loaded exports totaled 114,981 TEUs, down 7% from October 2025. “Exports have now declined year over year in six of the first 10 months here in 2026, as American farmers and manufacturers continue to face headwinds in overseas markets,” Seroka said. Through October, Los Angeles has handled 9,108,497 TEUs, 5% ahead of last year and 9% above its five-year average. Seroka said November volumes are also shaping up to be strong, raising the possibility of another annual record. “If December also delivers, I believe this could be the busiest year in our port’s 118-year history,” he said. Despite the historic volumes, a potential labor disruption and mounting rail delays threaten to complicate cargo movements at the neighboring ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The Pacific Maritime Association and International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26, which represents about 250 maritime watchmen at the ports, have extended contract negotiations through November 20 . The extension temporarily averts a walkout, but a strike remains possible if the two sides fail to reach an agreement. Although the watchmen represent a small portion of the waterfront workforce, a work stoppage could have a much broader impact. Other ILWU locals, including longshore workers in Local 13 and marine clerks in Local 63, have indicated they would honor Local 26 picket lines. A strike would come as both ports are already struggling with elevated intermodal container dwell times. Recent port data showed approximately 9,500 rail-bound import containers at Los Angeles had been waiting nine days or longer for on-dock rail transportation. At Long Beach, another 5,063 containers faced similar delays. Separate import dwell-time data from Los Angeles showed approximately 67% of containers moving through terminals within four days, while 11% remained five to eight days and 23% stayed nine days or longer. Logistics provider C.H. Robinson has identified a shortage of intermodal railcars in Southern California as a contributing factor to the slowdown. Trucking capacity is also under pressure. “Port congestion at LA and Long Beach due to increased import volume and reduced driver capacity continues to be highly elevated,” said Paul Brashier, vice president of global supply chain at ITS Logistics. “With congestion reducing the amount of containers a driver can execute daily, shippers should be prepared to add additional trucking capacity to navigate these conditions through Lunar New Year.” Any labor disruption could further extend container dwell times and create additional challenges for importers moving goods inland. Despite the operational pressures, Seroka remains optimistic about cargo demand heading into next year. After two visits to China and discussions with manufacturers, he said factories there are running at full capacity, with exporters anticipating strong shipments through the end of 2026 and into early 2027. The temporary easing of U.S.-China tariff tensions has provided some relief for shippers, while the extension of the suspension of U.S. port fees targeting Chinese vessels has removed another near-term source of uncertainty. Importers are also expected to accelerate shipments ahead of Lunar New Year, contributing to the elevated cargo flows. Still, the outlook remains vulnerable to further changes in trade policy, including potential Section 301 tariffs, the direction of U.S.-China negotiations and renewed tensions surrounding advanced semiconductor technology. There are also questions about how long American consumers can sustain the current pace of spending. High energy and food prices continue to pressure household budgets, while rising consumer debt raises additional questions about demand heading into 2027. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York recently reported that U.S. credit card balances reached a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter. Another source of cargo demand—and uncertainty—is the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Trade data provider ImportGenius has been tracking shipments of data center components and infrastructure moving through Los Angeles and Long Beach as technology companies expand their computing capacity across the United States. But questions about future projects, electricity availability and the political environment could influence how much equipment continues to move through the ports. “The big players in the AI space have been competing largely on the capabilities of their models,” said Lynn Hughes, lead analyst for the trade research team at ImportGenius. “Recent election results and limited grid capacity will cause investors in data centers to re-evaluate their exposure. But it’s very likely that the next area of competition is efficiency in training and inference.” For now, the Port of Los Angeles is closing out 2026 with record cargo momentum and the prospect of its busiest year ever. Whether that pace can continue into 2027 will depend not only on consumer demand and U.S.-China trade relations, but also on the ability of Southern California’s ports, railroads and trucking networks to keep freight moving. Saronic has awarded a contract worth more than $100 million to Norway’s Syncrolift to design and supply what the companies say will be the world’s largest shiplift at its planned $3 billion Port Alpha shipyard in Brownsville, Texas. The system will feature a 300-meter (984-foot) lifting platform with a capacity of 67,000 metric tons, more than twice the lifting capacity of the next-largest installation, according to Saronic’s announcement Thursday. Syncrolift, a subsidiary of Oslo-listed Nekkar ASA, will manage the project from its headquarters near Oslo. The company previously disclosed the contract on November 4 without identifying the customer, calling it the largest order in its history. Final delivery is scheduled for 2028. The massive shiplift will play a central role in Saronic’s plans to rethink how ships are built, allowing multiple vessels to be assembled and outfitted simultaneously on land rather than occupying traditional dry docks. Instead of building ships in fixed docks, Port Alpha is being designed around a production system in which large hull sections are assembled and vessels move between workstations. The shiplift and accompanying transfer system will allow completed ships to be moved from their construction positions into the water. The tandem lifting system will incorporate condition-monitoring technology and digital-twin controls to monitor operations throughout the lifting process. “The scope and scale of this shiplift is foundational to how the yard will operate,” said Doug Lambert, Saronic’s co-founder and chief operating officer. The approach is intended to reduce bottlenecks associated with traditional shipbuilding, where dock availability and limited waterfront space can constrain production. By moving more construction and outfitting work onto land, Saronic aims to increase the number of vessels that can be built simultaneously. The contract marks another major step in the development of Port Alpha, which broke ground on September 30 . Located at the Port of Brownsville, the shipyard will initially occupy 835 acres, with the potential to expand to nearly 4,400 acres. Saronic plans to invest more than $3 billion in the project, which it says could eventually support up to 10,000 direct jobs. The facility is being developed to build both autonomous and crewed vessels for commercial and defense customers, reflecting growing efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity amid concerns over the country’s declining share of global ship production. According to Saronic’s Port Alpha development plans , the initial phase will accommodate ships measuring up to approximately 850 feet, with future expansion potentially supporting vessels exceeding 1,200 feet. The company is targeting initial operations in 2028, with plans to eventually produce as many as 20 ships annually by 2035. Its first vessels are expected to be Landing Craft Utility vessels under a U.S. Navy contract. Saronic is also working with South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries as it develops its shipbuilding capabilities. The Syncrolift agreement highlights the role international suppliers are expected to play in the project, even as Saronic positions Port Alpha as a major investment in rebuilding domestic maritime manufacturing capacity. The contract was announced in connection with the Atlantic Future Forum, a gathering of defense, security and technology leaders focused on cooperation among allied nations. articles.title: Finland Detects Strike on Baltic Sea Russian Warship
articles.summary: Finland's military said on Thursday its forces had detected "a strike" on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, but that the security situation in the area remained stable.It was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused the strike.
articles.body: Finland Detects Strike on Baltic Sea Russian Warship Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Flavijus Piliponis Finland's military said on Thursday its forces had detected "a strike" on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, but that the security situation in the area remained stable. It was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused the strike. Estonian media reported on Thursday that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship and that it later returned to St Petersburg. "The Finnish Defence Forces detected... a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation," a spokesperson for the Nordic country's military said in an emailed statement to Reuters. Finland is not under any immediate military threat, the spokesperson added. The defence forces declined to provide further details about the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected. Ukraine has been sending waves of military drones towards Russia's northwest Leningrad region, which includes the city of St Petersburg as well as the Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet for commodities such as oil and grain. Some Ukrainian drones have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic region, leading to fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia and its ally Belarus. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania early on Wednesday issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response. The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia that extends eastwards to St Petersburg. (Reuters)

November 12, 2026 © Adobe Stock/PX Media Oil prices rose on Thursday by more than $1 a barrel, as continued disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and broader geopolitical tensions offset pressure from rising crude output that had sent prices lower in early trade. Brent futures were up $1.2 or 1.3% a barrel at $93.96 at 12:08 p.m. ET or 1508 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 53 cents or 0.6% at $87.06. Both benchmarks were still headed for a weekly decline. Prices fell early, and had been trading steady to lower before President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the US did not need a deal with Iran. "Those days have long since passed. "The tit-for-tat exchanges between Russia and Ukraine and attacks on shipping by the IRGC are beginning to add additional price pressure," said Timothy Snyder, chief economist at Matador Economics. In a potential breakthrough, a US envoy said Putin agreed to include European representatives in the next round of negotiations. In the US, crude stocks, gasoline and distillate inventories rose last week, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday. articles.title: New ultra-deep oil & gas discovery marks ‘major breakthrough’ in Bohai Sea
articles.summary: CNOOC has revealed an ultra-deep natural gas find in the central Bohai Sea, with a high-yield volcanic well testing at 800,000 cubic meters per day.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 12, 2026 · 1 minute ago New ultra-deep oil & gas discovery marks ‘major breakthrough’ in Bohai Sea CNOOC has revealed an ultra-deep natural gas find in the central Bohai Sea, with a high-yield volcanic well testing at 800,000 cubic meters per day. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Offshore platform (for illustration purposes) Source: CNOOC Chinese state-owned oil and gas giant China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) has made a high-yield natural gas discovery in volcanic rock more than 5,700 meters beneath the central Bohai Sea, opening doors to a new frontier for ultra-deep exploration in the region and bringing the company one step closer to building a trillion-cubic-meter gas province off the coast of China. CNOOC has drilled a high-yield volcanic oil and gas well in ultra-deep formations over 5,000 meters deep in Bohai, said to represent a major breakthrough in ultra-deep natural gas exploration offshore China. The well, which is adjacent to the Bozhong Sag , the largest hydrocarbon-rich sag in Bohai, encountered a cumulative total of over 120 meters of gas pay zone in volcanic formations and was completed at a depth of 5,770 meters. The well was tested to produce approximately 800,000 cubic meters (around 28 million cubic feet) per day of natural gas, uncovering promising exploration prospects in the offshore ultra-deep volcanic rocks and promoting the natural gas exploration process in the Bozhong Sag. " In recent years, CNOOC Limited has continued to strengthen theoretical innovation in deep and ultra-deep oil and gas enrichment in basins with high heat flow and strong activity, and to intensify research on key technologies. Exploration in China’s offshore areas has achieved a major leap from shallow to deep and ultra-deep formations. The success of this well has opened up a new play for offshore ultra-deep natural gas exploration and expanded the scope of deep oil and gas exploration in Bohai. It is of positive significance for accelerating the ultra-deep exploration process in Bohai and for building a major gas province of one trillion cubic meters in Bohai. " — Xu Changgui Chief Scientist and Chief Geologist of China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) Related Articles Business & Finance CNOOC’s 2026 run powered by 9 start-ups, 5 new oil & gas discoveries, and 23 appraisals 2 min read While the ultra-deep formations in Bohai are geologically complex, making reservoir prediction difficult, CNOOC has continued to make what it describes as breakthroughs in its theoretical understanding of offshore ultra-deep oil and gas exploration. The company independently developed key offshore deep multi-source broadband three-dimensional (3D) seismic exploration technologies and innovative methods for predicting high-quality reservoirs in ultra-deep buried hills. The Chinese player points out that its efforts enabled it to identify the favorable ultra-deep volcanic natural gas enrichment zones in the Bozhong Sag, discovering a high-yield oil and gas well, and marking significant progress in ultra-deep volcanic natural gas exploration in Bohai. articles.body: Contracts & Tenders November 12, 2026 · 7 minutes ago SLB on multi-year integrated drilling quest with European oil & gas operator SLB’s new assignment with Vår Energi aims to drive efficiency and performance across two rigs owned by Transocean and Odfjell Drilling. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Deepsea Bergen rig Source: Odfjell Drilling U.S.-headquartered energy technology giant SLB has landed a long-term integrated drilling job with Norway’s oil and gas company Vår Energi to provide services for two harsh-environment semi-submersible rigs in Norwegian waters, with extension options that could keep the company occupied through 2034. SLB has been selected by Vår Energi as its main integrated drilling services supplier for the Transocean Barents and Deepsea Bergen rigs on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), covering an initial four-year period, with four additional one-year extension options that could extend the scope through 2034. The two harsh-environment semi-submersibles will continuously drill exploration and development wells during this period. The U.S. giant explains that the integrated delivery model brings together technical expertise, digital workflows, and operational execution across the well delivery process. Torger Rød , Chief Operating Officer of Vår Energi, commented: “Creating greater value on the Norwegian Continental Shelf requires us to challenge traditional ways of working. By connecting planning and execution and bringing together expertise, technology and data, we can work across traditional boundaries to deliver wells faster, more predictably and with greater value.” SLB, which will be working closely with Vår Energi and other selected service and technology providers, will connect planning and execution, simplify interfaces, and use data to support faster decisions and more consistent well performance. This assignment expands the U.S. giant’s role in the Norwegian operator’s offshore operations, adding integrated drilling services to an established relationship spanning digital well and field development planning and subsea production systems through the OneSubsea joint venture. ND Maduemezia , President of Europe and Africa at SLB, noted: “We value the trust Vår Energi has placed in us. Our focus now is on differentiated execution, combining technology, technical expertise, operating discipline and digital capabilities to deliver consistently high performance at scale.” This comes shortly after SLB secured a 15-year deal with TotalEnergies for the deployment of coherent well planning and engineering solutions across the globe. articles.title: Port of Gothenburg eyes large-scale biogas bunkering in 2027
articles.summary: Sweden’s Port of Gothenburg is gearing up to launch a new LBG liquefaction plant next year to enable large-scale liquefied biogas bunkering.
articles.body: Ports & Infrastructure November 12, 2026 · 10 minutes ago Port of Gothenburg eyes large-scale biogas bunkering in 2027 Sweden’s Port of Gothenburg is gearing up to launch a new LBG liquefaction plant next year to enable large-scale liquefied biogas bunkering. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Artist’s impression of Nordion Energi’s biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg Source: Port of Gothenburg The Port of Gothenburg, which is perceived as the largest port in the Nordic countries, has tucked a new green transition milestone under its belt with the installation of a 500-cubic-meter storage tank for liquefied biogas (LBG). Built and owned by Nordion Energi and scheduled to open in the second quarter of 2027, Sweden's first grid-connected biogas liquefaction plant is set to unlock large-scale renewable bunkering for the shipping industry and supercharge the local green fuel value chain. The construction milestone for the biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg comes as the facility’s storage tank for LBG got installed. This renewable fuel with low climate impact is said to have the ability to replace fossil alternatives in several sectors. As a result, the interest in the fuel is growing rapidly, particularly in shipping. " Shipping’s transition requires a collaborative value chain. This facility strengthens the port’s position in renewable bunker fuels and makes it possible to offer LBG to the shipping sector on a larger scale. As we see more and more vessels on order for LBG operation, we also see strong potential for increased bunkering at the Port of Gothenburg. " — Therese Jällbrink Head of Renewable Energy at the Port of Gothenburg According to the Port of Gothenburg, groundworks, including foundations and base slabs, have been completed, and the LBG tank is the first of the plant’s key components to be installed. The tank, which arrived at the European port by vessel, has a volume of 500 cubic meters and weighs close to 140 tonnes. It will be able to store up to 200 tonnes of LBG once the facility is operational. Related Articles Alternative Fuels Port of Gothenburg hosts Swedish-produced biomethane bunkering pilot 2 min read " This is an important milestone. The facility is now really starting to take shape, and we are moving closer to our goal of being able to deliver LBG from the gas grid to shipping, heavy transport and industry. " — Carolina Wistén Head of Customer and Market, Gas Grid, at Nordion Energi The liquefaction plant, which will be the first in Sweden to be directly connected to the west Swedish gas grid, will create a new market for Swedish biogas producers that are, or want to become, connected to the gas grid. This facility, which is expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2027, will be capable of delivering 250 gigawatt-hours of LBG annually, equivalent to the consumption of 500 trucks or the bunkering of 50 vessels.
